## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Makkaṭajātaka* (Ja 173) is a short birth story preserved in the second book of the Pali Jātaka collection. Its framing narrative is located at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivered the story concerning a hypocritical or deceitful monk (*kuhakabhikkhu*) [Fausböll 1879]. The opening verse begins with the address, “Father, see! a poor old fellow”, and the commentary notes that the full background circumstances of the rogue monk are related in the *Uddālakajātaka* of Book XIV.

In the story of the past, an impudent monkey disguises himself in ascetic bark garments (*vakkalāni*) to practice deception, but is detected, driven off, and forced to cast off the robes and flee into the forest [Fausböll 1879]. The Bodhisatta, living as an ascetic, cultivates the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and gains rebirth in the Brahma realm (*brahmaloka*) [Fausböll 1879]. In the formal identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the deceitful monk was the monkey, his son Rāhula was the young ascetic (*tāpasakumāro*), and he himself was the senior ascetic [Fausböll 1879].
